targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a low, rounded, much-branched bush wider than tall, every stem and narrow leaf felted white-grey, paler and softer than the sagebrush around it; in summer covered in small yellow flower heads

description: A low, rounded, much-branched bush, usually knee high or less, whose stiff stems and narrow little leaves are felted with white-grey wool, so it looks paler and softer than the sagebrush it grows among. It has no spines. In summer the tips of its branches carry small clusters of narrow yellow flower heads, each of four tiny tubular flowers in a woolly cup, and its light seeds blow away on the wind. In Jackson Hole it grows in the dry sagebrush flats and hills, on gravelly and sandy soils, and it is one of the first shrubs back after a fire, sprouting from its roots. It is poisonous to sheep, and mule deer browse it mostly in winter.

season_notes.winter: Leafless grey-white twigs among the sagebrush; mule deer browse it on their winter range.
season_notes.spring: New woolly grey leaves; young shoots and buds are the most poisonous to livestock now.
season_notes.summer: Small yellow flower heads at the branch tips from late June into August.
season_notes.fall: Fluffy seeds blow off in the wind and the leaves drop; a burned flat greens with its sprouts.

range.where: the dry sagebrush flats, hills and ridges of Jackson Hole, on gravelly and sandy loams, thickest where fire has opened the sagebrush; western North America east of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada, from British Columbia to California and east to southwest Montana, Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico

notes: Big sagebrush (the template) is a grey Asteraceae shrub of the same steppe and height scale (itself a generated record, from coyote brush); horsebrush is lower, paler, deciduous and smooth-barked. Height 10-80 cm (Wikipedia), up to about 2 m (FEIS, which also calls the habit low); height_m 0.25-0.8 m is the drafter's. Many-branched, stiff semi-woody to woody stems, no spines (FEIS, Wikipedia). Leaves lance-shaped, to 4 cm, woolly or silver-haired (Wikipedia); 1-3 cm by 1-4 mm, long-lived primary leaves and short-lived secondary ones, dropping in autumn (FEIS); hence leaf_size_m 0.02, lanceolate and deciduous. The white-woolly stems with hairless strips are Wikipedia's; the pale grey colours are the drafter's from that. Flower heads 3-6 per cluster, each of 4 pale to bright yellow tubular flowers in 4 woolly phyllaries (Wikipedia), in small racemes at short branch tips (FEIS); flowering May-October (Wikipedia), from mid-June in British Columbia into September or October elsewhere (FEIS); June-August for Jackson Hole is the drafter's. Achenes 3-4 mm, wind-dispersed (FEIS); no berries block. Habitat (FEIS): dry open hills, ridges and plains on medium to coarse, gravelly or sandy loams; with sagebrush, pinyon-juniper and ponderosa pine; weedy, seral, not shade tolerant, very drought tolerant; Wyoming 1219-2743 m (FEIS); Wikipedia: sagebrush scrub, woodland and plains, mostly 1500-2700 m, reaching southwest Montana and Wyoming. Fire (FEIS): top-killed, sprouts rapidly from the root crown, seeds abundantly, can dominate burned sagebrush-grass and declines about 30 years after fire; hence disturbed 1.5 and shade 0.02. The Jackson Hole placing is from the brief; no National Park Service page read names horsebrush (the Yellowstone sagebrush steppe page names only sagebrushes). Animals (FEIS): poisonous to domestic sheep (liver damage, photosensitization, bighead; young shoots and buds worst); cattle not poisoned and mostly avoid it; mule deer browse it moderately in winter and lightly in spring (rated good on Wyoming winter range); pronghorn sparingly; elk fair in Wyoming; cover for small mammals and small birds (fair to good in Wyoming). Pronghorn is not in the library; the deer mouse stands in for the small mammals using it as cover. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stems, lean, leaf-on months, habitat weights and the flower size and colour are the drafter's judgement, not from a source.
